# Diagnosing Bugs

A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) to get a clear mental model of the relevant modules, and check ADRs in the area you're touching.

## Phase 1 — Build a feedback loop

**This is the skill.** Everything else is mechanical. If you have a **tight** pass/fail signal for the bug — one that goes red on _this_ bug — you will find the cause; bisection, hypothesis-testing, and instrumentation all just consume it. If you don't have one, no amount of staring at code will save you.

Spend disproportionate effort here. **Be aggressive. Be creative. Refuse to give up.**

### Ways to construct one — try them in roughly this order

1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug — unit, integration, e2e.
2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) — drives the UI, asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.

### Tighten the loop

Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:

- Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
- Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
- Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)

A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight — a debugging superpower.

### Non-deterministic bugs

The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not — keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.

### When you genuinely cannot build a loop

Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.

### Completion criterion — a tight loop that goes red

Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** — a script path, a test invocation, a curl — that you have **already run at least once** (paste the invocation and its output), and that is:

- [ ] **Red-capable** — it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring" — it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
- [ ] **Deterministic** — same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
- [ ] **Fast** — seconds, not minutes.
- [ ] **Agent-runnable** — you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.

If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop — jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.

## Phase 2 — Reproduce + minimise

Run the loop. Watch it go red — the bug appears.

Confirm:

- [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described — not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
- [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
- [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.

### Minimise

Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut — keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.

Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.

Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing** — removing any one of them makes the loop go green.

Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.

## Phase 3 — Hypothesise

Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.

Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.

> Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."

If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe — discard or sharpen it.

**Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it — proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.

## Phase 4 — Instrument

Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**

Tool preference:

1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Never "log everything and grep".

**Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.

**Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.

## Phase 5 — Fix + regression test

Write the regression test **before the fix** — but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.

A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.

**If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.

If a correct seam exists:

1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
2. Watch it fail.
3. Apply the fix.
4. Watch it pass.
5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.

## Phase 6 — Cleanup + post-mortem

Required before declaring done:

- [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
- [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
- [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
- [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
- [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message — so the next debugger learns

**Then ask: what would have prevented this bug?** If the answer involves architectural change (no good test seam, tangled callers, hidden coupling) hand off to the `/improve-codebase-architecture` skill with the specifics. Make the recommendation **after** the fix is in, not before — you have more information now than when you started.

The parser (`parseContact`, `gmail-sync.ts:119-133`) has two separate branches:
- `email:` (singular) → expects a **string** on the same line: `/^email:\s*(.+)$/`. Your line has nothing after the colon, so it doesn't match.
- `emails:` (plural) → the **only** branch that reads `- ` list items: `/^emails:\s*$/`.

Your list sat under the singular key, so **neither branch matched** and `contact.emails` came back `[]`. # Personal CRM

A text-based personal CRM built from email archives. Contact information is stored as markdown files with YAML frontmatter, organized by relationship type.

## Project Structure

```
client/              ~287 markdown files, one per client
colleagues/          ~8 markdown files, professional colleagues
friends/             ~20 markdown files, personal friends
mbox/                Gmail mbox exports (gitignored)
src/                 TypeScript scripts for data extraction
correspondents-filtered.csv  Curated list of 280 client emails/names
```

## Contact File Format

All contacts (clients, colleagues, friends) use the same markdown format with YAML frontmatter. Files live in the appropriate category folder (`client/`, `colleagues/`, `friends/`).

### Client files (generated from Heather's mbox + Mark's Gmail)

```markdown
---
last_name: Harris
first_name: Joshua
email: "josh@clearandloud.com"
last_updated: 2026-02-14
---

## Notes

Prefers async updates over calls. Mentioned wanting to revisit pricing in Q3.

## Mark's Email History

### 2026-01-15
- **Subject:** Re: Sprint Review Follow-up
  - Direction: To client
  - Summary: Mark followed up on the sprint review action items.
  - Thread: 1856015111163477742

## Email History

### 2026-01-15
- **Subject:** Re: Sprint Review Follow-up
  - Direction: From client
  - Thread: 1856015111163477742
  - Message-ID: <CAB1234@mail.gmail.com>
```

### Colleague/Friend files (from Mark's Gmail only)

```markdown
---
last_name: DeVilla
first_name: Joey
email: "joey@globalnerdy.com"
last_updated: 2026-02-15
---

## Mark's Email History

### 2025-03-10
- **Subject:** Re: Catching up
  - Direction: From friend
  - Summary: Joey suggested meeting for coffee next week.
  - Thread: 18a4f2c3d5e6f7a8
```

### Format rules

- Entries sorted **newest to oldest**, grouped by date
- `last_updated` in frontmatter tracks when the file was last modified
- **Direction** values: "To client/colleague/friend", "From client/colleague/friend", or "CC'd"
- **"## Notes"** section, when present, sits above "## Mark's Email History" and is authored by Mark, not generated from email data. Claude must treat it as read-only: never generate, edit, delete, or rewrite this section — leave it exactly as found. If a file has no "## Notes" section, don't add one.
- **"## Email History"** section (Heather's mbox data) exists only in `client/` files; uses Thread ID (decimal, Gmail's `X-GM-THRID`) and Message-ID (RFC 2822)
- **"## Mark's Email History"** section uses Thread ID (hex, from Gmail API) and a one-sentence Summary
- Filenames are slugified as `lastname-firstname.md`. Contacts with no known name use the email local part. Duplicate names get the email domain appended
- Contacts with multiple email addresses use `emails:` (list) instead of `email:` (string) in frontmatter

## Data Sources

### Heather's mbox (client/ files, "## Email History" section)

Client files were originally generated from an mbox export of Heather Uhl's email (former operations manager). The mbox contains emails from her accounts:
- heather.uhl@agilepainrelief.com
- heather.uhl@felicisholdings.com
- heather.uhl@smart-life-choices.com
- heatheruhl@gmail.com

### Mark's Gmail (all files, "## Mark's Email History" section)

Mark Levison's Gmail (mark@felicisholdings.com) is accessed directly via the Gmail API, using `npm run gmail-sync` (see Scripts below). Mark's email data is added to the "## Mark's Email History" section of contact files across all categories.

## Gmail Labels for Category Routing

Mark's Gmail uses labels to classify contacts into CRM categories:

| Gmail Label | CRM Folder | Description |
|-------------|------------|-------------|
| `consulting-apr-clients` | `client/` | APR consulting clients |
| `personal-friends` | `friends/` | Personal friends |

**How labels drive file creation:**
- When an email exchange involving a contact is found, check if the contact's email or thread has one of these Gmail labels applied.
- If the contact is labeled `consulting-apr-clients`, create or update their file in `client/`.
- If the contact is labeled `personal-friends`, create or update their file in `friends/`.
- If a contact already has a file in any category, update it in place regardless of labels.
- Contacts with no label match and no existing file should be flagged for Mark to classify manually.
- Note: `gmail-sync` only updates contacts that already have a file (it discovers files under `client/`, `colleagues/`, `friends/` rather than searching Gmail for unknown contacts) — creating a file for a brand-new contact is still a manual step.

## Full Repo Access

`mbox/`, `src/`, and the `npm run` scripts are all accessible to Claude:

- **`mbox/`** — Contains raw email exports with private correspondence. Claude may read/grep these files (e.g., to search for a contact's threads) but should treat the contents as sensitive and not copy more into markdown files than is relevant to the task at hand.
- **`src/`** — TypeScript scripts for mbox processing. Claude may read, write, and modify these scripts.
- **`npm run` commands** (`extract`, `filter`, `senders`, `clients`) — Claude may run these.

Claude's primary role is still working with the **markdown files in `client/`**, `colleagues/`, and `friends/`, and `correspondents-filtered.csv`, but Claude can now go directly to the mbox and scripts when a task calls for it instead of asking the user to do so.

## Scripts

All scripts use TypeScript via `tsx`. Install dependencies with `npm install`.

| Command | Script | Purpose |
|---------|--------|---------|
| `npm run extract` | `src/extract-correspondents.ts` | Scan mbox, produce `correspondents.csv` with all contacts (filtered by >3 threads spanning >3 months, since 2020) |
| `npm run filter` | `src/filter-correspondents.ts` | Filter `correspondents.csv` to remove automated/system addresses, producing `correspondents-filtered.csv` |
| `npm run senders` | `src/extract-senders.ts` | Extract unique senders from mbox (since 2025) |
| `npm run clients` | `src/generate-client-files.ts` | **Historic** — one-shot bootstrap that originally generated `client/` from mbox + `correspondents-filtered.csv`. Overwrites each file from scratch (no merge with existing content), so it would destroy hand-written `## Notes` sections and any `## Mark's Email History` data. Not expected to run again; do not run against the live `client/` directory. |
| `npm run search-mbox -- <contact.md>` | `src/search-mbox.ts` | Dump the full decoded text of every mbox thread that mentions a contact. Matches the contact's frontmatter address(es) case-insensitively anywhere in the raw message (headers or body), then prints all messages in each matched thread to stdout. |
| `npm run gmail-login` | `src/gmail-login.ts` | One-time OAuth login for Mark's Gmail API access; run before the first `gmail-sync`. |
| `npm run gmail-sync -- [contact.md ...]` | `src/gmail-sync.ts` | Incrementally update contact files from Mark's Gmail via the Gmail API. With no file args, scans every existing file in `client/`, `colleagues/`, `friends/`. Searches each contact's address(es), dedups against entries already in the file, optionally summarizes new messages with a local Ollama model, and merges (never overwrites) via `mergeContact` in `src/merge.ts`. `--dry-run` previews without writing; `--no-summarize` skips the Summary line. This is the live path for updating "## Mark's Email History" — replaces the old Claude Cowork/Gmail-connector workflow. |

The typical pipeline (historic, one-time bootstrap) was: `extract` -> `filter` -> (manual review of CSV) -> `clients`. Ongoing updates now go through `gmail-sync`, which merges instead of overwriting.

`search-mbox` is a standalone lookup tool, separate from that pipeline: pass it one contact markdown file (e.g. `npm run search-mbox -- client/chelynne-schram2.md`) and it prints matching threads — newest thread first, messages within a thread oldest→newest — for you to read or post-process.

## Technical Notes

- The mbox file is ~8 GB and gitignored. It lives in `mbox/`.
- All mbox scripts stream the file line-by-line to avoid memory issues.
- Scripts handle RFC 2047 encoded headers (Base64/Q-encoding), multiline header continuation, and comma-safe address parsing.
- The `generate-client-files.ts` script processes ~142k messages in about 2 minutes.
- Client filenames are slugified as `lastname-firstname.md`. Clients with no known name use the email local part. Duplicate names get the email domain appended.

## Gmail CRM Updates

Updating "## Mark's Email History" from Mark's Gmail is done via `npm run gmail-sync` (see Scripts above), not Claude Cowork. Run it with no arguments to sweep every existing contact file, or pass specific file paths to scope a run (e.g. by folder or a subset of files). It only updates contacts that already have a file; creating a file for a brand-new contact discovered via Gmail labels is still a manual step (see Gmail Labels for Category Routing above).
